sections.label: Overview
sections.content: Tailwebs was my first job, and it moved fast. What started as managing a CRM and running outreach campaigns quickly expanded into owning the go-to-market for two internal SaaS products — ShopAR (B2B) and Kaipo (B2C). Across both, I handled messaging, positioning, content, sales channels, user onboarding, feedback loops, and analytics. I learned by doing, iterated quickly, and by the end I was making independent product and growth decisions backed by data.

sections.label: Foundation: CRM & Outreach
sections.content:
My first ownership area was HubSpot. I learned the platform end-to-end and took over lead management — tracking, follow-ups, and pipeline hygiene. This led into outreach, where I was introduced to Dripify for LinkedIn and Apollo.io for email campaigns.
After a few weeks of learning the tools, I owned all campaigns end-to-end: planning, execution, tracking, and lead management. Content and messaging started with CMO sign-off and gradually became fully my responsibility as I got a handle on what worked.

sections.label: ShopAR: B2B SaaS GTM
sections.content:
ShopAR was Tailwebs' internal SaaS product — an Augmented Reality tool that let retailers place their products in AR via phone or an Image-to-3D feature. I was handed the marketing and GTM from the ground up.
My scope:

Positioning and go-to-market strategy
Content for website, in-app, email, and push notifications
Minor contribution to feature ideation


Once the product was ready, I moved into sales. We tested four channels: Email, Cold Calling, Ads, and Door-to-Door.

What the data showed: Both Ads and Door-to-Door produced results. I ran 4 weeks of door-to-door sales while the CMO ran ads in parallel. After 4 weeks, ads showed better returns — we cut the other channels and focused there.
I then owned user onboarding, the feedback loop, and cross-functional conversations with product and tech on what to improve — all running alongside my core Tailwebs responsibilities.

sections.label: Kaipo: B2C AI Companion
sections.content:
Kaipo was an AI companion product — fully B2C, which meant a different muscle. With ShopAR behind me, I came into this one with more confidence and a clearer sense of where to focus.
With lower direct user interaction than B2B, I shifted my time toward analytics and product thinking. I went deep on Mixpanel — building funnels, mapping user journeys, identifying drop-offs, and figuring out what to act on.

Example 1 — Onboarding drop-off: Initial sign-up flow had a ~75% drop-off rate. We prioritised Google Sign-In. Drop-off fell to 15%.


Example 2 — Retention: We had no hook to bring users back. Beyond improving chat quality, we introduced a "feelings" section — a live emotional state indicator for the AI companion. The light gamification element improved return rates.

The through-line across both products: use cases and decisions had to be grounded in data, not instinct.

sections.label: What Made It All Work
sections.content: Across both products and the core BDE work, the force multiplier was automation and AI tooling. Removing manual effort from repeatable tasks created the bandwidth to go deeper on strategy, messaging, and analytics — which is where the real impact was.

sections.label: THE PROBLEM
sections.content:
Planning a trip to Pondicherry, I searched for recommendations and hit a wall — every result was a bloated blog post with too much noise and not enough signal. I wanted a simple list of places with a Google Maps link. That gap was the product idea.

Digging deeper, I spotted a second problem: the internet was flooding with generic, AI-generated travel content. Trust was eroding. Travelers wanted human experiences, not algorithm output.

sections.label: Positioning & Differentiation
sections.content:
I positioned the product as a community-curated directory — the opposite of AI-generated content. To back this up with real data, I ran a 2-week community research exercise on Reddit across 5–6 cities, collecting genuine local recommendations. This wasn't just market research — it became the product's core differentiator.

Key positioning choice: "Community-curated" wasn't a tagline — it was a trust signal the audience immediately connected with. Early users didn't just approve; they started contributing unprompted, reducing my data-collection load organically.

sections.label: Go-to-Market: One Channel, Full Focus
sections.content:
With a full-time job, I had limited bandwidth. I made a deliberate GTM call: pick one channel and go deep on it. I chose Reddit — where the audience already was, asking for travel recommendations. I engaged genuinely on existing posts across all the cities on my site. What started as a daily activity scaled down to 2–3 sessions a week as the channel matured.

Result: 60–80 users a day from 30 minutes of weekly effort. 2,000 users in the last 30 days — entirely from one channel, zero paid spend.

sections.label: Product Evolution
sections.content:
The MVP was a minimal directory — city pages with place listings and Google Maps links. After launch, I identified two gaps: it felt sparse, and it didn't offer enough value to retain users. I iterated deliberately.

What I added: A city dashboard (daily budget, transport, best time to visit, recommended stay) to improve stickiness. Download and share list features for brand distribution. A map view for discoverability. I tracked usage on each and kept features that showed signal — even low usage — over vanity features that added nothing.

sections.label: Validation & Feedback Loop
sections.content: I built a feedback popup directly into the site to close the loop with users. 154 submissions collected. 152 positive, 2 negative. I treated this as the clearest signal that the core value proposition was working — and used it to stay focused on what was already resonating rather than chasing scope creep.

sections.label: Monetization Thinking
sections.content: I approached monetization with the same intentionality as the product itself. Google Ads would have been the obvious route — but it conflicted with the clean, trust-first experience I'd built. I ruled it out. Instead, I went with affiliate marketing, integrating it as a native product category within each city page rather than an intrusive popup. The experience stays seamless; the brand integrity stays intact.

sections.label: SEO & Long-term Growth
sections.content: Organic search was the long game. I started SEO activities from day one, knowing results would compound slowly. From near-zero impressions in January to ~30 per day in April, the curve is moving. Direct traffic is also climbing — a potential early signal of Google-driven discovery as authority builds.

sections.label: Overview
sections.content: What started as an unfocused Pinterest experiment turned into a 10M impression, 550K engagement channel — built without a budget, just iteration and analytics. Over two years, I taught myself Pinterest from scratch, used data to identify a winning niche (Indian travel content for women), A/B tested designs until two formats broke out, and scaled from there. The channel is now merged with Where In India, closing the loop on the one mistake I made early: having an audience with nowhere to go.

sections.label: How It Started
sections.content: I wanted to grow a Pinterest account and did what most people do — followed trends. For the first 5–6 months I used Pinterest Trends to create pins across random categories. No niche, no strategy, no vision. Just post and hope.

sections.label: The Analytics Turning Point
sections.content:
As I got more comfortable with the platform and its analytics, a clear signal emerged: travel content was significantly outperforming everything else — and specifically resonating with Indian audiences and female users.

The decision: Stop spreading thin across topics. Double down on Indian travel content for a defined audience. I renamed the account to Travel India Now and fully committed to the niche.

sections.label: Creative Iteration & What Worked
sections.content:
Pivoting to travel content didn't instantly produce results. The early phase was heavy on experimentation — testing formats, layouts, and design variations to find what drove impressions. Out of many attempts, two pin designs consistently outperformed everything else.

The learning: Creative is a variable, not a constant. I tested until the data told me what worked, then doubled down on those two formats. That decision is what drove the channel to scale.

sections.label: The Gap I Missed
sections.content:
With growing impressions and engagement, there was one critical thing missing: a destination. I had no website or landing page to send traffic to, which meant zero outbound clicks. An audience was arriving and leaving with nowhere to go.

The lesson: Distribution without a funnel is just vanity metrics. Impressions mean nothing if there's no next step for the audience.

sections.label: Closing the Loop
sections.content:
The Pinterest account is now merged under the Where In India brand and pointed to whereinindia.online. Content creation has restarted under the new name, this time with a full funnel in place — impressions convert to site visits rather than dead ends.

Where it stands now: This is effectively a second learning curve — rebuilding audience trust and momentum under a new brand, but this time with the strategic foundation that was missing the first time around.
